title: ALMA and the Milky Way
caption: An ALMA antenna under the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: One ALMA antenna looks small beneath the Milky Way, which winds across the sky above the Atacama Desert in northern Chile. It is one of 66 dishes forming the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array.

The array is designed to observe the Universe at wavelengths between infrared light and radio waves, a range the eye cannot see. Light at these wavelengths carries information about some of the coldest regions of the Universe, the places where new stars are only just forming. It also helps astronomers learn about the earliest galaxies.

ALMA's dishes are spread across the high Atacama plateau. In this photograph, though, just one of them is set against our own galaxy, dwarfed by the sweep of the Milky Way snaking across the dark sky above it.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at an ESO site, in visible light. The camera settings and colour processing are not published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye can, so the Milky Way and faint stars appear brighter and richer than they would to someone standing there.

explore: The photograph was taken by M. Claro. The Milky Way seen overhead is our own galaxy, which contains the kind of cold clouds where stars form that ALMA was designed to study.
alt: A single dish antenna under the winding band of the Milky Way in a desert sky.
